parts.text: With their spindly legs and geometric heads, they look more like miniature spacecraft than anything living on Earth. But

, or simply phages, are among the most abundant biological entities on the planet.

These microscopic agents are viruses that can infect and kill bacteria, offering an intriguing alternative to antibiotics at a time that drug-resistant infections are

global health.

Despite decades of research, however, scientists still know surprisingly little about how most phages work. Many of their genes have functions that remain a mystery, limiting their potential in medicine and elsewhere.

Now, our new research offers a way to

them in greater detail. We’ve developed a method to pinpoint which genes phages need to function, and to insert new genetic material into their genomes within days.

This might eventually help researchers engineer phages that are better at attacking

bacteria – opening up possibilities for treating infections that conventional antibiotics struggle against.

Why phages are making a comeback

Long before antibiotics became the standard treatment for bacterial infections, doctors were using phages to

them.

Phages were first used in this way a century ago. But with the arrival of antibiotics, inconsistent results from early phage treatments and the onset of the Cold War, their medical use declined in Western countries.

In his 1945 Nobel Prize

, Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin, warned that bacteria could develop resistance to antibiotics. His warning proved prescient.

As new antibiotics were developed, resistant bacteria emerged, helped by the overuse and

of these drugs. Today, antibiotic resistance is projected to contribute to more than eight million deaths annually by 2050, prompting renewed interest in phage-based treatments.

Despite their growing use in medicine and agriculture, much of what we know about phages comes from a small

of well-studied examples. Their vast diversity, and the functions of many of their genes, remain largely unexplored.

Like humans, phages have genomes containing genes that carry instructions for making

. These proteins determine how the viruses function, including how they infect bacteria and reproduce.

To investigate phage gene function, scientists need tools that can boost our understanding and turn new knowledge into practical applications.

Bridging the knowledge gap

phages can be time-consuming, work only with certain bacteria, or require detailed knowledge of the phage’s genome.

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Aboriginal astronomical knowledge explains celestial movements and their connections to life on Earth.
Scientists are developing ways to select valuable soil samples from the Martian moon Phobos.
An ancient Arabian lakeshore provides evidence of human life in a landscape once much greener than today.
Bacteria-infecting viruses may offer new ways to tackle antibiotic resistance.
questions.explanation: 把标题与全文各段的中心内容连起来判断主旨，避免把同一主题下的其他话题当成本文重点。
questions.evidence: Typically, transposons carry an antibiotic resistance gene, allowing bacteria that receive them to survive antibiotic treatment.

questions.prompt: What is one potential medical use of the phage discovery?
options: Replacing every existing medicine immediately
Improving treatment for infections that resist conventional antibiotics
Preventing all infections without further testing
Making bacteria completely immune to every virus
